method.title: A clock instead of a theodolite
method.mini: A flat-earth project films a star being cut off by a mountain crest. At that second the observer, the crest and the star lie on one line, and an almanac turns the time into the star's altitude. The clock part works.
method.text: A flat-earth project called the Celestial Theodolite films a star being occulted by a distant mountain [1]. At that instant the observer, the crest and the star lie on one straight line, so the star's altitude, known to arcseconds from an almanac for the stated second [2], is also the elevation angle of the crest. Nothing is measured with an instrument: the clock says when, and the almanac turns the when into an angle. The claim is that on a plane, where every horizontal is parallel, that one line makes the same angle at both ends. The published targets run from 8.8 to 130.7 km. The elevation is enlarged in the drawing.
method.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: occultation times that match the flat crest angles rather than the globe's, across the published cases.
rate.title: What the clock buys
rate.mini: A star loses altitude at up to 15.041 arcseconds per second of clock. So a clock good to one second is ten times finer than the angle in dispute: the method's timing is not its weak point.
rate.text: How fast a star loses altitude: 15.041″ per second × cos φ × sin A, where φ is the latitude and A the star's azimuth from north. It is fastest due east and west, zero due north and south. The sidereal rate, 15.041° per hour, is 15.041 arcseconds per second of clock [1], which is what makes the method cheap: one second of clock error is a tenth of the effect at the shortest published range, and under a hundredth at the longest. Anywhere below about 60° of latitude, on a star setting near the west, a clock good to one second is ten times better than the angle in dispute. The drawing is schematic.
rate.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: star altitudes changing at a rate other than 15.041″ per second × cos φ × sin A.
predict.title: What the two models predict: zero, or γ
predict.mini: At the same second, ask the observer and the crest for the star's altitude. On a plane their horizontals are parallel: the difference is exactly zero. On a globe their verticals diverge by the angle between them, γ = s/R.
predict.text: Take the two ends of the line, the observer and the crest the star is grazing, and ask each for the star's altitude at the same second. On a plane the two horizontals are parallel, so the difference is exactly zero, with no free parameter. On a globe the two verticals diverge by the central angle γ = s/R, so the same straight line makes two different angles, differing by γ. The two heights cancel out of the difference, which is what makes it worth measuring. A federal survey crew observed the same quantity over 70 to 93 km lines in 1977 [1]. The drawing is schematic.
predict.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the two altitudes agreeing exactly over long distances.
rule.title: The method's own rule
rule.mini: One line of sight, three stations on it. On a plane every horizontal is parallel to every other, so the one line makes the same angle at each station. That is the rule the method relies on.
rule.text: The method rests on one rule: on a plane every horizontal is parallel to every other, so one straight line of sight makes the same angle with the horizontal at every station it passes through. The drawing shows three stations on one line, each reading the same angle a. The method uses this rule to carry the star's altitude from the observer to the crest. The drawing is schematic.
rule.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one line of sight measured at the same angle from distant stations.
pole.title: The same rule, carried to the pole star
pole.mini: Carry the method's own rule along a direction whose angle is known: the celestial pole, on the horizon at 0° for an observer on the equator. On a plane it must then sit at 0° everywhere. From Paris it stands at 48.9°.
pole.text: Apply the method's rule to a direction whose angle is already known somewhere: the fixed point of the sky, which an observer on the equator sees on the horizon, at 0°. A line horizontal at one station is horizontal at the next if the horizontals are parallel; apply it again and again, and the fixed point sits at 0° everywhere on Earth. From Paris it is at 48.9°, and Polaris marks it to 0.6°. No instrument, no second observer, no clock and no software are needed, and the discrepancy is 2,930′. The drawing is schematic.
pole.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the celestial pole on the horizon from every latitude.
objection.title: The simplest objection, built from the method itself
objection.labels: The rule|The rule, one direction later
objection.mini: The method assumes that one line makes the same angle at every station. Apply that to the celestial pole, horizontal at the equator: it would be on the horizon everywhere. From Paris it stands 48.9° up.
objection.text: The method carries an angle from one station to the next, on the assumption that every horizontal is parallel to every other: one line, the same angle at each station. So carry it in a direction whose angle is already known: the fixed point of the sky, which an observer on the equator sees on the horizon at 0°. A direction horizontal at one station would be horizontal at the next, and again at the next, so the fixed point would sit at 0° everywhere on Earth. From Paris it stands at 48.9°, and Polaris marks it to 0.6°. There are two ways out: either the horizontals are not parallel, or the rule the method uses is not the one it claims. The drawings are schematic.
objection.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the celestial pole seen on the horizon from Paris.
residual.title: Which crest angle does the star match?
residual.mini: From the timed second, an almanac gives the star's altitude. From maps and heights, each model gives the crest's angle. The two crest angles differ by s/2R, 35′ at 131 km. The star cannot sit on both.
residual.text: One number is measured: the second at which the star is cut by the crest. From it an almanac gives the star's altitude [1], which does not know which model you hold. From the published coordinates, trigonometry gives the crest's elevation angle, a different one for each model: arctan((H − h)/s) on a plane, the same minus s/2R on a globe. Subtract, and the leftover is each model's residual. The two crest angles differ by s/2R, which is 35′ at 131 km, so the star's altitude cannot sit on both. The drawing is schematic.
residual.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: star altitudes landing on the flat crest angle, case after case.
bars.title: One case, asked four ways
bars.mini: One published case, run through each model with and without refraction. The bars are the residuals, so shorter is better. The case is named above; the arithmetic is entirely from the project's own sheet.
bars.text: One case from the project's own workbook [1], named above the text, asked four ways: each model, with and without the almanac's refraction correction [2], and in each the crest angle reduced the same way as the star's altitude. The bars are absolute residuals between the measured second and each model's prediction, so shorter is better. Every number comes from the sheet; only the subtraction is done here. Across all cases on file, the globe with refraction comes out closest.
bars.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the flat bars shorter than the globe's across the cases.
box.title: Which model fits the published readings
box.mini: Every usable case in the project's own workbook, run through both models with refraction. The globe's median miss is about 2′; the plane's about 13′. The numbers are named above.
box.text: Both studies in the project's own workbook [1], over every usable case on file, with the numbers given above the text: the residual of each model against the measured second, with the almanac's refraction applied at both ends [2]. Smaller is closer to what was measured, and the median is the figure to read first, since one badly identified crest moves a mean and leaves a median alone. The globe with refraction comes closest, with a median of about 2′; the plane with refraction is next, at about 13′. The dots beyond the whiskers are cases where both models miss together, the signature of a misidentified crest rather than of either shape.
box.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: flat residuals with the smaller median over the project's own cases.
rsym.title: Solving the published data for the radius
rsym.mini: Run every case backwards: solve for the radius each observation implies. Three reductions give three answers. Only the one that treats the star and the crest the same way means anything.
rsym.text: Every case can be run backwards: instead of asking whether 6,371 km fits, solve for the radius each observation implies. Three reductions are possible. The first uses the difference of two altitudes the project's software computed on a globe, and lands on 6,371 km by construction. The second pairs a map-based crest angle with a geometric star altitude when the occultation happened in the apparent direction; that mismatch returns a radius near 3,000 km. The third fixes the mismatch and nothing else, with the standard refraction coefficient k = 0.13 [1]. Only cases beyond 20 km are used, where the two models differ by more than a crest error. The drawing is schematic.
rsym.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: radii that grow without limit, as a plane requires.
radius.title: The Earth's radius, from a flat-earth dataset
radius.mini: The flat-earth project's own occultation timings, reduced consistently, give the Earth's radius. The median of 28 cases beyond 20 km is named above: close to 6,371 km, not infinity.
radius.text: The same box plot as the residuals, now for the radius each case implies, with the accepted 6,371 km as a vertical line; the result is named above the text. Three reductions are shown. The first only checks the transcription, since the project's software computed its altitudes on a globe. The second, the method's default, pairs a geometric star altitude with an apparent occultation and lands near 3,000 km, a globe of the wrong size, not a plane. The third treats star and crest alike, with k = 0.13 [2], and it is the one to argue with. All data are the project's own [1]. A plane would need an infinite radius.
radius.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: radii from the consistent reduction that grow without limit.
trend.title: The flat model's miss follows the curvature
trend.mini: Beyond 20 km, the flat model's miss grows with the curvature term (1 − k)s/2R, case after case, with a correlation of 0.97. The globe's misses stay flat. The next shot, 24 November, has a predicted place on each.
trend.text: The 28 cases beyond 20 km from the project's workbook [1]. The flat model's miss tracks the curvature term (1 − k)s/2R, with k = 0.13 [2], not a fitted line, with a correlation of about 0.97, while the globe's misses show no trend. The figures are named above the text. So the two boxes are also a prediction: an independent shot, planned for 24 November, 208 m of height over 54.1 km, with a solar disc as the ruler instead of a clock, must land at 12.4′ on the plane's box and at zero on the globe's. If the plane is right, the two marks swap places.
trend.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the 24 November shot landing at zero on the plane's box and 12.4′ on the globe's.
shoot.title: The 24 November shot, minute by minute
shoot.mini: What a dense solar filter will show from the viewpoint on 24 November: the Sun's disc, and the terrain only where it cuts into it, at true angular scale. Black: the globe's skyline. Blue: the extra ridge the plane requires.
shoot.text: A pre-registered observation: what a dense solar filter will show, minute by minute, from the chosen viewpoint on 24 November, with the Sun's disc as the ruler, 32.4′ wide. The terrain appears only where it cuts into the disc, at true angular scale. The black silhouette is the globe's skyline; the blue band is the extra ridge a plane requires. The profile is sampled every 0.1° of azimuth, the resolution of the terrain model, so the facets are data, not smoothing. Each frame is centred on the disc: it is the ridge that climbs through it.
shoot.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the photographed ridge reaching the blue band.
frames.title: The 24 November shot, frame by frame
frames.mini: The same prediction as a strip of frames: the Sun sinking behind the far ridge on 24 November, at true angular scale. The globe's skyline in black, the plane's extra ridge in blue.
frames.text: The pre-registered 24 November observation as a set of frames: the Sun, 32.4′ across, sinking behind the far ridge, at true angular scale. The black silhouette is the skyline the globe predicts; the blue band is the extra ridge the plane requires. The profile is sampled every 0.1° of azimuth, the terrain model's resolution. A near crest at 16 km, where the models barely differ, controls the method. The photograph will show one or the other.
frames.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the Sun cut by the ridge at the height of the blue band.
